items.title: [theguardian.com] More than 120 climate scientists urge House to reject energy permitting bill
items.content_html: More than 120 climate scientists urged the U.S. House to reject a sweeping energy permitting bill that the Senate passed 62-33 on Nov. 19, warning it could lock in fossil-fuel projects while weakening environmental safeguards. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten federal reviews and make it harder to challenge some projects in court; its supporters say faster approvals could help connect clean power and lower electricity costs. The House is expected to take up the measure after the Thanksgiving recess, but no vote date has been announced. Lawmakers also face year-end legislation, including government funding due by Dec. 11. If the House passes it, the bill would go to President Donald Trump, whose administration has endorsed it.

items.content_html: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will suspend all cobalt exports from Nov. 30 until further notice, its strategic minerals regulator, ARECOMS, announced on Nov. 23. The government says it is responding to falling prices, weak global consumption and rising inventories. The DRC supplies nearly three-quarters of the world’s cobalt, used in batteries for electric vehicles and consumer electronics. The suspension is due for review four months after it takes effect. Kinshasa previously replaced an export halt with quotas. Industry participants warn that restricting shipments may not clear the glut if copper mining continues to produce cobalt as a byproduct while demand remains weak.

items.title: [ft.com] England's 5,258 heat deaths spur calls for climate adaptation
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An estimated 5,258 heat-associated deaths in England in summer 2026, a record, have intensified calls to prepare homes, health services and public infrastructure for rising temperatures. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) warned that climate change will make extreme heat longer, more frequent and more intense. The estimate covers May to September and remains provisional because death-registration data are incomplete. The summer was also dry: drought was declared across Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires damaged parts of the country. The agency said heat protection should start early in the season because people and public services may be less prepared for heat episodes in May and June. It also urged longer-term adaptation alongside emissions cuts.

items.title: [windpowermonthly.com] Scottish floating wind project reserves 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines
items.content_html: Green Volt, a planned floating offshore wind farm off Peterhead, Scotland, has reserved manufacturing capacity for 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines rated at more than 15 megawatts each. The project has consent for up to 560 megawatts and would supply electricity to the UK grid. The reservation is a procurement step, not a final turbine supply contract, and Siemens Gamesa says further milestones remain. Green Volt’s developers also signed a letter of intent with the Port of Aberdeen for anchor and mooring operations at Aberdeen South Harbour, supporting a proposed £15 million package for infrastructure and supply-chain work. The project secured key consents and a 400-megawatt UK government Contract for Difference in 2024, but still needs further contracts and investment before construction.

In France, BW ESS and local developer Wattmen plan to develop about 500 megawatts of battery projects over three years, with at least four hours of storage per site. In the United States, utility-scale battery capacity reached nearly 52 gigawatts by June 2026. U.S. developers are competing with gas peaker plants, while French batteries could earn revenue from wholesale power, balancing services and capacity markets. Japan’s storage market faces uncertainty over whether strong early revenues from ancillary services can sustain projects over their 20-year lifetimes, Umer Sadiq said.

items.title: [pv-magazine.com] Chinese maker brings foldable off-grid solar EV charger to Australia
items.content_html: Chinese portable solar equipment maker Gaotu Innovation has introduced a roof-mounted, off-grid electric-vehicle charger in Australia that combines a foldable solar array with up to 1,600 watts of input and a 2.5-kilowatt-hour battery. Gaotu says the system can provide up to 80 kilometres of daily driving range without grid power and is aimed at drivers travelling in remote areas or camping. The company says the battery buffers solar input and supplies regulated alternating-current power to a vehicle. The unit can also provide backup power during mains outages. Gaotu offers the system to Australian distributors and says it can customize versions for local partners.

items.title: [ArchDaily] COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities
items.content_html: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

items.title: [energytracker.asia] COP31 fossil-fuel deadlock leaves energy shift to voluntary pledges
items.content_html: United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft that omitted a direct reference to moving away from fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil-fuel-dependent states opposed such language. Delegates adopted no new overarching political direction on fossil fuels, while separate voluntary initiatives continued, including an electrification pledge backed by more than 90 countries. A proposal to expand carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne scale by 2035 was also disputed. Global operating capture capacity was about 68 million tonnes a year in mid-2026, while deployment across Asia remains limited. Countries adopted a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme, but the mechanism intended to put it into operation remained underdeveloped. The International Maritime Organization’s 176 member states are due to discuss a shipping emissions framework on Nov. 30 that could establish global carbon pricing and binding measures.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UN climate summit ends without pact as fossil fuel dispute stalls talks
items.content_html: The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to resolve disputes over fossil fuels and climate finance. The talks ran about two days past their scheduled close, making COP31 the longest COP conference on record. The final draft omitted an explicit reference to fossil fuels, prompting the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable island states to reject it. The draft referred indirectly to the 2023 COP28 commitment to transition away from fossil fuels but did not spell out a pathway or reaffirm the wording. Oil-producing countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, resisted explicit references to fossil fuels, while poorer countries objected that the proposal did not set concrete funding levels for adaptation. COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen said fossil fuels and finance were the main obstacles; summit president Murat Kurum said he would not put forward a replacement draft. Countries agreed on separate measures, including a program to support workers and communities through the energy transition and a plan to assess adaptation progress. More than 80 countries backed Türkiye’s proposed goal of raising electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, but the goal was not part of an adopted overarching pact. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on possible reforms to the consensus-based negotiating process. The next summit is scheduled for Addis Ababa.

items.title: [Common Dreams] 'COP31 Was a Colossal Failure': Longest UN Climate Summit Collapses Without Deal
items.content_html:
The longest United Nations Climate Change Conference on record ended in overtime on Sunday, with the governments gathered in Türkiye for COP31 unable to reach an agreement on tackling the fossil fuel-driven global emergency.

The Turkish and Australian governments hosted the conference in Antalya. According to The Guardian, Australia's minister for climate change and energy, Chris Bowen, told reporters outside the plenary room that he hadn't slept for three days.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that's very disappointing," Bowen said, hours after the latest draft drew a fresh wave of criticism. "Ultimately, looking back, many parties who are people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts, on reflection those red lines were not able to be met."

The European Union, Panama, and small island nations were among those that rejected the proposal. Explaining the EU's position, the Irish climate and environment minister, Darragh O'Brien, said that "it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels."

While Big Oil-backed US President Donald Trump has ditched the Paris Agreement and declined to send a delegation to COP31, even though his country is the largest historical climate polluter, other major petroleum producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia lobbied against mentioning fossil fuels. Panama's climate minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told Politico that "the world is hostage to petroleum producers. That is the truth... And they will not stop."

In the lead-up to the conference, scientists warned that temporarily surpassing the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C threshold for temperature rise this century, relative to preindustrial levels, is now inevitable, and the world is barreling toward "an irrecoverable overshoot" of that target absent a rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions.

Jasper Inventor, head of the Greenpeace International delegation at COP31, said that "it's bitterly disappointing to leave without a clear outcome or a credible pathway to end fossil fuels. We stopped a bad deal that favors fossil fuels, but leaving without a deal is still a failure for communities on the climate frontlines. As always, it is the world's most vulnerable communities who bear the consequences of this failure. We've run out of time to avoid overshoot, but we can still keep 1.5°C alive."

Climate campaigners from around the world joined Inventor in expressing frustration that "COP31 has failed to deliver any meaningful outcomes on climate action," as Oxfam International climate change policy lead Nafkote Dabi put it after two weeks of talks. "Shame on rich polluting countries for once again turning their backs on communities fighting for survival in a climate crisis they did little to cause. Shame on the presidencies for prioritizing profits and ego over progress."

"And shame on all the countries that stubbornly blocked and distracted from discussions meant to deliver crucial funding to people watching their homes swallowed by floods, their crops wither in droughts, and their lives upended by deadly heat," said Dabi. "Instead of implementation, COP31 has delivered yet another victory for rich polluting countries and fossil fuel interests. The co-presidencies—who both remain heavily invested in fossil fuels and are profiting from climate destruction—attempted to broker a decision without a single mention of fossil fuels in favor of false solutions."

View on X

Nikki Reisch, a director at the Center for International Environmental Law, explained that "the proposed cover decision did not advance the provision of climate finance, said nothing about the root cause of the crisis, and made no mention of states' legal obligations to prevent and repair climate harm, as clarified by the International Court of Justice. On loss and damage, it fared no better as it offered little more than expressions of deep concern about mounting impacts. And a text that welcomed a scale-up of future fantasy fixes like carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies and proven-to-fail industry favorites like carbon capture and storage (CCS), without so much as a whisper about fossil fuels, would have been a massive giveaway to polluters."

Calling out the hosts, Global Climate and Health Alliance executive director Jeni Miller stressed that "the rightly rejected 'Antalya Pact' comes as climate change compounds this year's super El Niño, causing severe droughts in Fiji and Bolivia, extreme flooding in the western US, and wildfires in Southeast Asia, and putting millions of additional people at risk of hunger or famine."

Amiera Sawas, head of research and policy at the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, highlighted that "while Global North countries rejected the outcome on the basis that there was no language on transitioning away from fossil fuels, these same countries have not themselves presented serious or credible phaseout plans, nor do they intend to support others in their transitions. Many wealthy countries continue expanding fossil fuel extraction despite their international legal obligations, while developing countries carrying unpayable debt can't plan an exit at all."

"The EU and some of its most powerful member states have blocked progress or, worse, reneged on past commitments," Sawas continued. "Demanding the words 'fossil fuels' in the cover text while blocking mandated agenda items and pointing fingers at developing countries is acting in bad faith. We need real commitments to a fair and financed phaseout of fossil fuels that delivers on the Paris Agreement, not collapses it. That means a just transition, where those most responsible pay their fair share and workers, communities, and Indigenous peoples have a meaningful say in what it looks like."

View on X

Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa, declared that "this has been the worst ever COP, and its collapse needs to be a wake-up call for the world. Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook."

Romain Ioualalen, global policy lead at Oil Change International, similarly asserted that "this will go down as one of the worst COPs in history. COP hosts Australia and Türkiye have failed to steward the negotiations. This sad stalemate only benefits fossil fuel interests while people and communities will continue paying the highest price for the crisis they didn't create."

"Don't fall for the EU's attempt to portray themselves as heroes. They are the ones who are largely to blame for this result... But let's be clear: The outcome on the table was dangerous," he continued, welcoming the proposal's defeat. "Countries failed to rise to the moment, but we refuse to lower the bar. The countries and communities fighting for climate justice are not backing down, and the road to COP32 in Ethiopia must be about action."

Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, also emphasized how bad the final deal was: "After decades of broken pledges and hollow commitments, an agreement built on yet more empty promises would have been unforgivable and no substitute for the transformative action we urgently need. So the dramatic rejection of the presidency's final text by some, though underscoring the lack of consensus that's been reached, restores some level of faith in its recognition that a deal of this caliber is no deal at all."

"What matters now is not when governments reconvene, it's how they do so," he argued. "The world doesn't need more meetings with woolly commitments. We need global governments, including the UK, to come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver. That means cutting emissions fairly at home, transitioning our economies in a way that leaves no one behind, and providing the public climate finance so desperately needed to protect people, livelihoods, and our planet from unimaginable harm."

View on X

Savio Carvalho, head of campaigns and networks at 350.org, also looked ahead: "You'd think that in the middle of the worst fossil fuel crisis in history, after a year of devastating wildfires, floods, and collapsing glaciers, world leaders would finally rise to the moment. But they didn't. We averted a truly bad outcome because many countries stood up to the fossil fuel industry and rejected dangerous distractions. But we still left COP31 without a clear plan to exit coal, oil, and gas. There's no real money on the table to help countries survive the climate breakdown that is already at our doorstep."

"The world needs governments with the courage to stand with people and the planet, even when the fossil fuel industry pushes back," Carvalho added. "This isn't the end. We'll keep pushing until governments end the age of fossil fuels. Every meeting and every decision in the year ahead counts. The time for delay is over."

items.title: [downtoearth.org.in] COP31 draft sets 2035 electrification goal without clean-power rules
items.content_html: A new COP31 draft sets a collective ambition to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 and expand carbon capture, use and storage to gigatonne scale by that year. The text, drawn up by the Turkish and Australian summit co-presidents in Antalya, does not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels or require the additional electricity to come from renewables. Governments had yet to approve it. The electrification target concerns energy used across the economy, not a renewable-power quota. The latest draft also drops an earlier version’s direct link to tripling renewable capacity by 2030 and doubling the annual rate of energy-efficiency improvement. The draft postpones decisions on a 2035 adaptation-finance goal and the timing of future Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assessments, while noting those reports’ relevance to the 2028 global stocktake. The closing plenary was repeatedly delayed on Sunday as negotiators considered whether to adopt the text.

items.title: [farmer.pl] Farmers turn to soil and water strategies as climate extremes intensify
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Farmers and researchers are testing soil, irrigation and crop-management measures as drought, flooding and extreme heat strain agriculture in Poland, Sweden and Senegal. At a Polish agriculture conference, experts said drought resilience depends on assessing soil conditions and improving long-term water retention. A Swedish research project is assessing a system designed to store water in dry periods and release it during floods. In Senegal, farmers and agricultural workers report hotter planting seasons and fewer hours in the fields, while shared irrigation along the Senegal River has become vital. The Swedish project will test the system under different climate scenarios and develop implementation guidance. Researchers say its effects on soil ecosystems and nutrient releases still need study.

items.title: [grist.org] Michigan court leaves state renewable energy siting rules largely intact
items.content_html: The Michigan Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge by dozens of townships to Public Act 233, the 2023 law that lets the state approve certain renewable energy projects when local zoning rules exceed the law’s standards. The order leaves most of that framework in place, but the court also ruled that any local government affected by a project—not only the government with zoning authority—can qualify as an affected local unit. The justices have not resolved a separate dispute over when a 30-day deadline begins for local officials to tell developers they have a qualifying ordinance. They scheduled arguments for the January 2027 session and directed the parties to file briefs in December and January. The order does not approve or reject any specific energy project.
